coredata.dc:description: In the current research, ZnFe2O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe2O4, ZnFe1.90Bi0.10O4, ZnFe1.95Ce0.05O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 magnetic nanoparticles were synthesized to remove the BPA (bisphenol A) from contaminated water through photocatalytic performance. The synthesized nanoparticles were characterized by powder XRD, UV-DRS, FT-IR, SEM-EDAX, VSM and XPS. From the XRD results it was observed that the particle size ranged from 38.26 to 30.18 nm. UV-DRS showed the band gap value ranging from 1.94 to 1.04 eV for the fabricated magnetic nanoparticles. Under 250 W UV-light irradiation, degradation of BPA using Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 nanoparticles were 90.09 and 91.25% in 180 min with the rate constant of (k) 0.02250 and 0.02365 min−1, respectively. The reactive species responsible for photocatalytic degradation were hydroxy radicals and superoxide radicals. 87.89% and 88.91% of degradation was observed after three cycles using Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 nanoparticles. The outcomes indicated that Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 nanoparticles show good stability for BPA degradation.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: In the current research, ZnFe2O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe2O4, ZnFe1.90Bi0.10O4, ZnFe1.95Ce0.05O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 magnetic nanoparticles were synthesized to remove the BPA (bisphenol A) from contaminated water through photocatalytic performance. ce:section.ce:para: Now-a-days, with the rapid development in the present-day industry, a different kind of organic contamination namely Endocrine Disrupting Compounds (EDC) are being released into water which is unavoidable [1]. Specifically, Bisphenol A (4,4′-(propane-2,2- diyl)diphenol) which is found in plastics, bottles, paper, packaging and epoxy resins [1–3]. About 5.5 million tons of BPA was used per annum [4]. Though it is known to be one of the notable ED compounds [5,6], and harmful to human health, agriculture and environment, degradation of bisphenol A is difficult due to its stable structure. At present, Bisphenol A (BPA) is being discharged into the water vigorously, which creates the importance of elimination of BPA [2,7]. In recent times, numerous techniques have been identified to expel BPA from water, including physical elimination development [8], chemical oxidation [6,9] and biodegradation [10]. Among these treatment methods, chemical oxidation is known to be an efficient and easy technique for the clean-up of the wastewater [5,9,11,12].

In the past decades, spinel ferrite oxide (MFe2O4, where M=Cu, Co, Mg, Zn, Ni, Mn) magnetic nanoparticles were used for data storage, magnetic resonance imaging, sensors, catalysis and in solar cells [13–17]. ZnFe2O4 nanoparticles in particular are well known for the structural, optical, electrical, magnetic, antibacterial and catalytic properties [18–22]. Zinc ferrite is a normal spinel structure with the general formula AB2O4, where Zn2+ ions are in tetrahedral (A) position and Fe3+ ions are in octahedral (B) positions. In recent years, many researchers have been reporting substituted zinc ferrite nanoparticles such as Zn1-xMgxFe2O4 [18], Zn1-xCoxFe2O4 [19], Cu1-xZnxFe2O4 [20], ZnFe2-xNdxO4 [21], ZnFe2-xBixO4 [22], ZnFe2-xCexO4 [23], ZnFe2-xCrxO4 [24], ZnFe2-xLaxO4 [25], ZnFe2-xSmxO4 [26], Ni0.5Zn0.5WxFe2-xO4 [27], Zn1-yCayFe2-xGdxO4 [28], ZnFe2O4/Ag/PEDOT [29], ZnFe2O4@ZnO [30], ZnFe2O4- MM/RGO [31] and ZnFe2O4@TiO2 [32] for various applications. To the best of the author's knowledge, there is no work focused on copper, bismuth co-doped and copper, cerium co-doped zinc ferrite (Zn1-yCuyFe2-xMxO4, (M=Bi & Ce)) nanoparticles. Copper, bismuth and cerium-based materials have various applications in catalysis, photoluminescence, sensors, mechanical stability, laser, LED applications, and biological applications [33,34]. Earlier, many synthetic techniques have been reported for the synthesis of ZnFe2O4 nanoparticles. When compared to other methods, the solution combustion method has many advantages such as shorter preparation time, better crystallinity, high energy efficiency, homogeneity and simplicity.

The current communication reports the fabrication of copper, bismuth co-doped and copper, cerium co-doped zinc ferrite (ZnFe2O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe2O4, ZnFe1.90Bi0.10O4, ZnFe1.95Ce0.05O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4) nanoparticles using solution combustion method. The synthesized nanoparticles were analyzed using different instrumentation methods such as powder XRD, UV-DRS, FT-IR, SEM-EDAX and VSM. For the first time, the prepared co-doped ferrite nanoparticles were analyzed for the degradation of bisphenol A (BPA) under UV-light irradiation.
All the chemicals employed in the current study were purchased from s.d fine. It was ensured that they were of analytical reagent grade and used without further treatment or purification.

ZnFe2O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe2O4, ZnFe1.90Bi0.10O4, ZnFe1.95Ce0.05O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 nanoparticles were synthesized via a solution combustion route. For the preparation of zinc ferrite 2.97 g of Zn(NO3)2. 6H2O and 8.08 g of Fe(NO3)3·9H2O was dissolved in double distilled water, 3.5 g of C2H5NO2 was then added to the solution and it was continuously stirred at 80 °C for 15–20 min towards the formation of a homogeneous solution. After that, the homogeneous solution was burnt in a furnace at 350 °C for 5–7 min. Finally, the attained samples were ground well and calcined at 700 °C and 900 °C for 4 h. The same procedure was followed for other compounds with stoichiometric quantities of Cu(NO3)2·3H2O, Bi(NO3)3·5H2O or Ce(NO3)3·6H2O

The structure and crystal phase of the fabricated ferrite nanoparticles were authenticated by powder XRD (D8 advance BRUKER Germany). The functional group and surface morphology of the synthesized ferrite nanoparticles were analyzed using FT-IR (SHIMADZU) and SEM (ZEISS EV018). The optical and magnetic properties of the prepared nanoparticles were analyzed by UV-DRS (JASCO V670) and VSM (LAKESHORE 7410).

The photocatalytic performance of the synthesized magnetic nanoparticles were estimated by the degradation of Bisphenol A (BPA) in an aqueous solution. A 250 W mercury lamp was used as the source for the UV-light. In this experiment, 50 mg of synthesized magnetic nanoparticles was added into 50 ml of aqueous solution (BPA 10 ppm). Then, the suspension was mechanically stirred in dark condition for 60 min to attain the equilibrium between the magnetic nanoparticles and the BPA. The sample (catalyst and BPA solution) was irradiated with UV-light for 180 min. A total of 3 ml of the solution was taken at regular intervals of time and the magnetic nanoparticles were removed with the help of external magnet and the filtrate was analyzed using a UV–visible spectrophotometer (JASCO V-730). The percentage of degradation was calculated using the formula [35,36]
(1)
P e r c e n t a g e
o f
d e g r a d a t i o n = C o − C t / C o × 100
Where C 0 and C t is initial and final concentration of the BPA solution after degradation.

Fig. 1 explains the powder X-ray diffraction pattern of ZnFe2O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe2O4, ZnFe1.90Bi0.10O4, ZnFe1.95Ce0.05O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 magnetic nanoparticles fabricated by solution combustion. From the powder XRD pattern it was discovered that the synthesized magnetic nanoparticles have a cubic crystal system and further the peaks were then matched with the JCPDS file no. 82–1042. No impurities in the peaks were noticed in the XRD pattern which shows the pure single-phase structure of ZnFe2O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe2O4, ZnFe1.90Bi0.10O4, ZnFe1.95Ce0.05O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 (Fig. 1a). However, the high intensity peak (311) in ZnFe2O4 slightly shifted to higher angle with the copper, bismuth and cerium doping. This indicates the incorporation of Cu, Bi and Ce in the zinc ferrite (Fig. 1b). Krutiga et al. reported that this shifting is because of the recurrent structural distortion due to doping [37]. Based on Debye–Scherrer's equation and FWHM (full-width at half-maximum), the average crystallite size was calculated and it was found to be 38 nm, 37 nm, 36 nm, 35 nm, 32 nm and 30 nm for ZnFe2O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe2O4, ZnFe1.90Bi0.10O4, ZnFe1.95Ce0.05O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4, respectively. The introduction of copper, bismuth and cerium caused the reduction in the crystallite sizes. Similar results are observed by Yan et al. [38]. A high volume of energy is needed to complete the substitution. The source of energy is at the expense of the crystallization and hence reduction in particle size is noticed [38].

Fig. 2 demonstrates the FTIR spectra of the magnetic nanoparticles in the range 400–2000 cm−1. To study the functional groups in the ZnFe2O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe2O4, ZnFe1.90Bi0.10O4, ZnFe1.95Ce0.05O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 FT-IR analysis was utilized. The FT-IR spectra (Fig. 2) of zinc ferrite nanoparticles displayed two strong characteristic peaks at 405.15 cm−1 and 520.48 cm−1, which correspond to the stretching vibrations of the spinel in the tetrahedral voids and the oxygen-metal vibrations in the octahedral voids [22]. A similar perception was noted for the doped and co-doped compounds as well.

The optical property of the prepared magnetic nanoparticles was examined through the UV-DRS analysis. Fig. 5 shows the band gap energy of ZnFe2O4 (1.94 eV), Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe2O4 (1.87 eV), ZnFe1.90Bi0.10O4 (1.64 eV), ZnFe1.95Ce0.05O4 (1.62 eV), Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 (1.56 eV) and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 (1.04 eV) calculated using Tauc equation. The band gap value of ZnFe2O4 was found to be 1.94 eV, which is comparable to the value described by Tatarchuk et al. [19] and Rashmi et al. [26]. From the above outcomes, it can be noted that the introduction of copper, bismuth and cerium caused the reduction in the band gap energy (red-shift) compared to zinc ferrite. A similar observation was noted by Tatarchuk et al. [19] and Rashmi et al. [26] for cobalt doped zinc ferrite nanoparticles and samarium doped zinc ferrite nanoparticles, respectively.

Fig. 6 demonstrates the magnetization of copper, bismuth co-doped and copper, cerium co-doped zinc ferrite nanoparticles. The magnetization values of ZnFe2O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe2O4, ZnFe1.90Bi0.10O4, ZnFe1.95Ce0.05O4, Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 nanoparticles were found to be 63.42, 59.17, 37.22, 29.38, 49.15 and 43.38 emu/g, respectively. The magnetization was highest for ZnFe2O4 and doping and co-doping of Cu, Bi and Ce reduced the magnetization. It was noticed that there was a reduction in the saturation magnetization for ZnFe1.90Bi0.10O4 and ZnFe1.95Ce0.05O4, but co-doping of bismuth, copper and cerium (Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 nanoparticles) increased the magnetization. According to the Neel's theory [22,23], the magnetism of ferrite nanoparticles is the total of magnetic moment of each ion in the octahedral and tetrahedral sites. The reason for decrease in saturation magnetization (ZnFe1.90Bi0.10O4 and ZnFe1.95Ce0.05O4) could be due to the distribution of non-magnetic ions Bi3+, Ce3+ in the octahedral site which pushed some of the Fe3+ (5 µʙ) ions in the tetrahedral site. The magnetic moment of Cu2+ ion (1.73 µʙ) is larger than Zn2+ (0 µʙ), hence co-doping increased the saturation magnetization (Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4).

Fig. 7 demonstrates the Zn 2p, Cu 2p, Fe 2p, Bi 4f and Ce 3d and O 1 s XPS spectra of Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 nanoparticles. For Zn 2p, two peaks associated with Zn2+ can be seen at1020.03 eV (2p3/2) and 1043.86 eV (2p1/2) [39,40]. The Cu 2p consists of two spin-orbit doublets 2p3/2 (932.83 and 934.77 eV) and 2p1/2 (953.16 and 955.11 eV) which indicates the presence of Cu2+ions. In addition, the four corresponding ‘shake-up’ satellites (denoted at Sat.) are observed at 939.93, 942.12, 960.32 and 962.07 eV are correspond to the Cu2+ions [41,42]. The peaks in the XPS spectrum of Fe 2p3/2 (709.0 and 711.59 eV) and 2p1/2 (720.88 and 723.06 eV) and the corresponding satellite peak at 717.20 eV are exhibited due to Fe3+ ions [39,41,43]. The four peaks at 156.76, 158.11 eV and 162.27, 163.57 eV are corresponding to Bi 4f7/2 and Bi 4f5/2 of Bi3+ ions present in the nanoparticles [41,43]. The Ce 3d peaks can be fitted into nine peaks due to its variable oxidation states (Ce3+ and Ce4+). 880.17 eV (Ce3+), 887.04 eV (Ce4+), 890.26 eV (Ce4+), 894.38 eV (Ce4+), 898.21 eV (Ce4+) and 902.03 eV (Ce4+), 905.55 eV (Ce3+), 908.74 eV (Ce4+), 914.10 eV (Ce4+) are assigned to Ce 3d5/2 and Ce 3d3/2 of Ce3+, Ce4+ ions present in the nanoparticles [44–47]. The characteristic peaks of O 1 s spectra at 527.78, 529.16 and 530.94 eV are associated to the lattice oxygen in metal oxygen bonds, hydroxyl groups and water adsorbed on the surface [48,49]

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of Cu2+, Bi3+ and Ce3+ dopant
ce:section.ce:para: Fig. 8b displays the pseudo-first-order kinetics for the removal of BPA using synthesized nanoparticles under UV-light illumination within 180 min. The rate constant (k) values calculated are 0.00368 min−1 (without catalyst), 0.00872 min−1 (ZnFe2O4), 0.01038 min−1 (Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe2O4), 0.01169 min−1 (ZnFe1.90Bi0.10O4), 0.01480 min−1 (ZnFe1.95Ce0.05O4), 0.02250 min−1 (Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4) and 0.02365 min−1 (Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4). From the above outcomes, it is noticed that Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 (0.02250 min−1) and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 (0.02365 min−1) nanoparticles exhibited higher rate constant which might be owing to the co-doping of Cu, Bi and Ce which enhances the rate constant values.

We noted a higher removal efficiency (90.09% and 91.25%) and a high rate constant (0.02250 min−1 and 0.02365 min−1) for BPA using Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 nanoparticles within 180 min under UV-light. Therefore, the Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 nanoparticles were selected for further studies (effect of catalyst, concentration and scavengers).

The dosage of magnetic nanoparticle is an essential factor in the photocatalytic activity since it impacts the BPA photodegradation powerfully. Fig. 8c and d demonstrates the effect of the of quantity of the Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 nanoparticles (25 mg–75 mg) for the BPA degradation under UV-light in 180 min. 75 mg of nanoparticles exhibited a higher photocatalytic activity than 50 mg and 25 mg (Fig. 8c and d). The difference in percentage of degradation with 50 mg and 75 mg was not too high. Hence we fixed lower quantity of the catalyst 50 mg for further optimization. The photodegradation efficiency of the catalyst is tabulated in Table 2 . The rise in the magnetic nanoparticle dosage is useful for the creation of photogenerated e − - h + (electron – hole), and reactive oxygen species responsible for the degradation of the molecule [55]. From the above results it is determined that 50 mg is the optimum quantity for the BPA photodegradation.

The impact of BPA concentration on the photocatalytic performance of the Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 nanoparticles are estimated by varying the BPA concentrations from 5 ppm to 15 ppm utilizing 50 mg of the magnetic nanoparticles in 180 min under UV-light (Fig. 9 a and b). The results are tabulated in Table 2 which displays that the percentage of the removal of BPA decreases with the increase in the BPA concentration. This could be due to the two probable reasons. (i) When BPA concentration rises, extra molecules are adsorbed on the surface of the nanoparticles and the quantity of radicals formed on the nanoparticles surface decreased [56]. (ii) 15 ppm of BPA is obstructing the photocatalytic active sites on the nanoparticles and hence decreasing the photons interaction [57].

To deduce whether h + (hole), ·OH (hydroxyl radical) or ·O2 ‒ (superoxide radicals) reactive species contributed to the degradation of BPA, the radical trapping experiments were carried out in the presence of EDTA (ethylene diamine tetraacetic acid, trap the h +), IPA (isopropyl alcohol, trap the ·OH) and BQ (benzoquinone, trap the ·O2 ‒). As revealed in Fig. 9c and d, the degradation of BPA by Zn0.5Cu0.5Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.5Cu0.5Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 nanoparticles reduced significantly from 90.09% & 91.25% to 76.23% & 78.95%, 43.78% & 45.71% and 17.57% & 19.23% in the presence of EDTA, IPA and BQ. These results help to conclude that ·OH and ·O2 ‒ are the significant radical scavengers for BPA photodegradation. It might be seen that BPA photodegradation rate was lesser with IPA (·OH) and BQ (·O2 ‒) than when degraded without scavenger and EDTA. These conclusions are in line with those noticed by previous literature [58].

Based on the results of several experiments, a schematic representation of the mechanism for the degradation using Zn0.5Cu0.5Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.5Cu0.5Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 magnetic nanoparticles is given in Scheme 1 . When magnetic nanoparticles are irradiated by UV-light, e − (electrons) are excited from the VB (valence band) to the CB (conduction band). The e −which get transferred to the CB of magnetic nanoparticles will react with O2 to produce ·O2 ‒ radicals. Also, h +in the VB of magnetic nanoparticles will react with H2O or OH‒ to produce active species such as ·OH radicals. The highly reactive ·O2 ‒ and ·OH are in charge of the photodegradation of BPA which may be broken into the mineral acids, CO2 and H2O [59].

In addition to UV-Visible analysis for the photograded BPA solution, HPLC was recorded [59] using Waters high performance liquid chromatography with a C18 column and mobile phase of methanol/acetonitrle/water (50:30:20) at a flow rate of 0.5 ml/min [54] and the wavelengths are 227 nm and 275 nm. HPLC chromatograms showing the reduction in the peak intensity of BPA at 180 min using Zn0.5Cu0.5Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.5Cu0.5Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 nanoparticles are given in Fig. 10 . The HPLC chromatogram obtained in 180 min shows that no BPA peak can be observed. Similar observation was made by Yang et al. [4] and Chen et al. [60].

In order to decrease the cost of the materials and to study the stability of the Zn0.5Cu0.5Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.5Cu0.5Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 nanoparticles, reusability of the catalyst was carried out three times. The outcomes of photodegradation are given in Fig. 10. From 1st to 3rd run, the degradation of BPA was decreased from 90.09% to 87.89% and 91.25% to 88. 91% using Zn0.5Cu0.5Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.5Cu0.5Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 nanoparticles respectively (Fig. 11 a). The stability of both the nanoparticles were confirmed using powder XRD after the third cycle (Fig. 11b). The pure crystalline structure of Zn0.5Cu0.5Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.5Cu0.5Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 nanoparticles were not modified after three recycles (Fig. 11b). After the photodegradation of BPA, it could be finalized that the nanoparticles possess good stability.

In summary, un-doped, doped and co-doped zinc ferrite magnetic nanoparticles have been successfully synthesized through the solution combustion technique. The prepared nanoparticles were characterized using various instruments. From the XRD results pure single- phase formation of un-doped, doped and co-doped zinc ferrite nanoparticles were observed. In addition, XRD and DRS analysis showed the crystallite size reduction and band gap energy reduction when Cu, Bi and Ce was introduced. It was found that co-doped zinc ferrite (Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4) nanoparticles exhibited a higher BPA removal efficiency than the doped and un-doped zinc ferrite nanoparticles. The photogenerated hydroxyl radical and superoxide radical was found to be the major reactive species for the BPA photodegradation. Moreover, the stability of the Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.90Bi0.10O4 and Zn0.50Cu0.50Fe1.95Ce0.05O4 nanoparticles were also confirmed. A possible photodegradation pathway of BPA has been explained.
